title: Tail Latency and Request Hedging
oneLiner: Why the slowest 1% of calls decides how fast a large system feels, and how a backup request fixes it for a few percent more load.
keyTakeaway: Measure latency in percentiles, not averages: p99 is the time that 99% of requests beat. When one user request fans out to many servers and waits for all of them, it is as slow as the slowest one, so rare hiccups become common: with 100 backends that are each slow 1% of the time, 63% of user requests hit at least one slow call. A hedged request (send a second copy if the first is late, keep whichever answers first) cuts the tail sharply for a few percent more load, as long as the work is safe to do twice and the servers have spare capacity.
explanation:
Latency is how long one request takes, and it is never a single number. Most requests are quick and a few are very slow, so the average hides the part users complain about. Percentiles describe the whole spread: sort every request's time, and the p50 (the median) is the one in the middle, the p99 is the time that 99% of requests are at or below, and the p999 (the 99.9th percentile) is the one in a thousand. A service handling 1,000 requests a second produces a p999 request every second, and a user who loads a page that makes 50 calls will meet the p99 often. That is why latency targets are written as "p99 under 200 ms" rather than "average 40 ms", and why the slow end of the distribution is called the tail.

Two traps when you work with percentiles. First, they don't average: the mean of ten servers' p99 values is not the p99 of the fleet, so monitoring systems keep histograms (bucketed counts, or sketches such as HdrHistogram and t-digest) and merge those instead. Second, a percentile needs enough samples: a p999 computed from 500 requests is just the slowest one.

Tails come from things every real machine does now and then: a garbage collection pause, a request queued behind a burst of others, a background job such as log compaction, a noisy neighbour sharing the same host, a dropped packet that waits for a TCP retransmission timeout, a cold cache after a deploy. You can make each one rarer, but at scale you can't make them all go away, so large systems are built to tolerate them.

Fan-out is what turns a rare hiccup into a common one. A search query, a news feed or a product page often sends one request to many servers in parallel (one per shard, or one per microservice) and waits for every answer. If each call is slow with probability p, all N calls are fast with probability (1 - p)^N, so the user request is slow with probability 1 - (1 - p)^N. With p = 1% and N = 100 that is 1 - 0.99^100, about 63%. The server's p99 has become the user's median. This example is from Jeff Dean and Luiz Barroso's 2013 paper "The Tail at Scale", which most of this lesson follows.

A hedged request attacks the tail directly. Send the request to one replica; if no answer has arrived after a short delay, send the same request to a second replica, use whichever answer comes back first and cancel the other. If the delay is the call's p95 latency, only the slowest 5% of calls get a second copy, so the extra load is about 5%, while the slow calls now take roughly the delay plus a normal call instead of a full hiccup. The paper reports a Google benchmark that read 1,000 keys spread over 100 servers: hedging after 10 ms cut the 99.9th percentile from 1,800 ms to 74 ms while sending just 2% more requests.

A tied request goes further for delays caused by queueing. The client sends the request to two servers at once (in practice a millisecond or less apart), each copy tagged with the other server's identity. Whichever server starts executing first tells the other to cancel its copy. The request waits in the shorter of two queues, but in almost every case it is executed only once. Tied requests don't help when the slowness happens during execution, such as a GC pause after the work started; hedging does.

Both techniques have rules. Hedge only work that is safe to do twice: reads, or writes protected by an idempotency key (a unique request id the server uses to recognise a repeat). A hedged payment charges the card twice. Cap the extra load with a budget, because when the slowness comes from overload, more copies make it worse: always sending two copies doubles the work and can push busy servers into the steep part of the queueing curve. Other tail tools from the same paper: return a good-enough answer once most shards reply, replicate hot items more, and temporarily take a slow machine out of rotation.

The simulator is a teaching model with seeded randomness, so the same settings always give the same numbers. Each call normally takes 5 to 15 ms of work plus a short wait. With the chance you choose, a call hits a hiccup of 100 to 1,000 ms: half of those are waits in a queue before the work starts, half are pauses during the work. The utilization slider sets how busy the servers already are, and any duplicated work raises it, stretching every queue wait by the factor (1 - old utilization) / (1 - new utilization), the shape of a simple queue. It runs 5,000 user requests for each setting and reports nearest-rank percentiles.
